metadata.title: Lecture 6.5 - RMSProp: Divide the Gradient by a Running Average

nodes.name: Error surface for a linear neuron
nodes.statement: For a linear neuron with squared error, the error surface is a quadratic bowl: vertical cross-sections are parabolas, and horizontal cross-sections are ellipses.
nodes.statement_clean: The error surface of a linear neuron with squared loss is a quadratic bowl in weight space.

nodes.name: Mini-batch gradient descent
nodes.statement: Update the weights using the gradient computed on a small subset (mini-batch) of the training cases rather than on the full dataset; the extreme one-case-at-a-time version is called online learning.
nodes.statement_clean: An algorithmic schema that updates weights on small batches rather than the full dataset.

nodes.name: How learning goes wrong with steepest descent on a ravine
nodes.statement: On a long narrow ravine the gradient is large in directions where only a small step is wanted and small in directions where a large step is wanted, so steepest descent oscillates across the ravine and may diverge if the learning rate is too big.

nodes.name: Basic mini-batch gradient descent with learning-rate schedule
nodes.statement: Mini-batch SGD with hand-tuned learning-rate adaptation: increase or decrease the rate based on whether the error is falling smoothly, and turn it down toward the end of training using a held-out validation set.
nodes.pseudocode: Guess an initial learning rate $\epsilon$. Repeat: compute the gradient on a mini-batch and update $w \leftarrow w - \epsilon \nabla E$. If the error oscillates wildly or grows, decrease $\epsilon$; if the error falls slowly and consistently, increase $\epsilon$. Near the end of training, decrease $\epsilon$ to remove fluctuations; turn $\epsilon$ down when the validation error stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Be careful about turning down the learning rate too soon
nodes.statement: Turning down the learning rate reduces random fluctuations in the error caused by mini-batch noise (giving a quick win) but also slows learning, so it should not be done too early.

nodes.name: Initializing the weights
nodes.statement: Break symmetry by initializing weights to small random values, and use incoming weights proportional to $1/\sqrt{\text{fan-in}}$ to avoid overshoot when the fan-in is large.

nodes.name: Shifting and scaling the inputs
nodes.statement: For steepest descent, transform each input component to have zero mean and unit variance over the training set; this reshapes the elongated quadratic error surface so descent behaves better.

nodes.name: Decorrelate the input components via PCA
nodes.statement: For a linear neuron, decorrelate inputs by Principal Components Analysis: drop the components with smallest eigenvalues and divide the remaining components by the square roots of their eigenvalues, converting the axis-aligned elliptical error surface into a circular one.

nodes.name: Common plateaus mistaken for local minima
nodes.statement: With too-large initial learning rates, hidden units saturate and their derivatives become tiny, producing a plateau; in classification networks a similar plateau arises when the network learns to output the class prior before exploiting the inputs.

nodes.name: Four ways to speed up mini-batch learning
nodes.statement: Use momentum, use separate adaptive learning rates per parameter, use rmsprop (divide the rate by a running magnitude of recent gradients), or adapt a curvature-aware optimization method.

nodes.name: Momentum method
nodes.statement: Use the gradient to change a velocity rather than the position of the weight, then update the weight by the current velocity; this damps oscillations along high-curvature directions and builds speed along consistent gradient directions.
nodes.pseudocode: At each step $t$: $v(t) = \alpha\, v(t-1) - \epsilon\, \partial E/\partial w(t)$ and $\Delta w(t) = v(t) = \alpha\, \Delta w(t-1) - \epsilon\, \partial E/\partial w(t)$. Use a small $\alpha$ (e.g. 0.5) at the start of training and raise it (e.g. 0.9 or 0.99) once the large initial gradients have decayed.

nodes.name: Terminal velocity on a tilted plane
nodes.statement: On an error surface that is a tilted plane, the momentum method reaches a terminal velocity $v(\infty) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\left(-\epsilon\, \frac{\partial E}{\partial w}\right)$, which can be much faster than plain gradient descent when $\alpha$ is close to 1.

nodes.name: Nesterov-style momentum (Sutskever 2012)
nodes.statement: First take a big jump in the direction of the previous accumulated gradient, then measure the gradient at the resulting point and apply a correction; better to fix a mistake after making it than before.
nodes.pseudocode: Step 1: jump in the direction of the previous accumulated gradient. Step 2: evaluate the gradient at the new location and add it as a correction.
nodes.origin_citation: Inspired by Nesterov 1983; form due to Sutskever 2012 (unpublished)

nodes.name: Per-connection adaptive learning rates (local gains)
nodes.statement: Multiply a global learning rate by a per-weight local gain $g_{ij}$ that grows additively when consecutive gradients agree in sign and shrinks multiplicatively when they disagree, ensuring rapid decay of large gains during oscillation.
nodes.pseudocode: Update: $\Delta w_{ij} = -\epsilon\, g_{ij}\, \partial E/\partial w_{ij}$. If $(\partial E/\partial w_{ij}(t))(\partial E/\partial w_{ij}(t-1)) > 0$ then $g_{ij}(t) = g_{ij}(t-1) + 0.05$, else $g_{ij}(t) = g_{ij}(t-1) \times 0.95$. Clip $g_{ij}$ to a reasonable range, e.g. $[0.1, 10]$ or $[0.01, 100]$.

nodes.name: Tricks for adaptive learning rates
nodes.statement: Limit the gains to a sensible range, prefer full-batch or large mini-batches so gradient sign-changes are not sampling noise, and combine adaptive rates with momentum (using sign agreement between current gradient and velocity, Jacobs 1989); adaptive rates only handle axis-aligned effects, while momentum handles arbitrary directions.

nodes.name: rprop (resilient backpropagation)
nodes.statement: For full-batch learning, ignore gradient magnitudes and use only the sign: increase the per-weight step size multiplicatively when consecutive gradient signs agree and decrease it multiplicatively when they disagree; clip step sizes to a fixed range.
output: Updated weights with adapted per-weight step sizes
nodes.pseudocode: If signs of last two gradients for weight $w$ agree, multiply its step size by a factor (e.g. 1.2); otherwise multiply by a factor < 1 (e.g. 0.5). Limit step sizes (e.g. between $10^{-6}$ and 50). The weight update is the step size times the sign of the gradient.

nodes.name: Why rprop fails on mini-batches
nodes.statement: SGD relies on averaging gradients across successive mini-batches, but rprop ignores magnitudes: a weight receiving $+0.1$ on nine batches and $-0.9$ on the tenth would be incremented nine times and decremented once by the same amount, so it would drift instead of staying near its starting value as desired.

nodes.name: Combine rprop's robustness with mini-batch averaging
nodes.statement: Find an update rule that retains the robustness of rprop (insensitive to gradient magnitude variations across weights) while preserving the efficiency of mini-batches and the effective averaging of gradients across mini-batches.

nodes.name: MeanSquare running average of squared gradients
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t) = 0.9\, \mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t-1) + 0.1\, \big(\partial E/\partial w\,(t)\big)^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: An exponential moving average of the squared gradient with decay 0.9 and innovation weight 0.1.

nodes.name: RMSProp
nodes.statement: Mini-batch optimizer that divides each weight's gradient by the square root of a running mean of its squared gradients, forcing the per-weight normalization to be stable across adjacent mini-batches.
nodes.pseudocode: Initialize $\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, 0) = 0$. For each mini-batch, compute $g = \partial E/\partial w$, update $\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t) = 0.9\, \mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t-1) + 0.1\, g^2$, and update $w \leftarrow w - \epsilon\, g / \sqrt{\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t)}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Tijmen Tieleman, unpublished (described in Hinton's Coursera lecture, 2012)

nodes.name: Compute mini-batch gradient
nodes.statement: Compute the gradient $g = \partial E/\partial w\,(t)$ on the current mini-batch.

nodes.name: Update running mean of squared gradient
nodes.statement: $\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t) = 0.9\, \mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t-1) + 0.1\, g^2$.

nodes.name: Normalized weight update
nodes.statement: $w \leftarrow w - \epsilon\, g / \sqrt{\mathrm{MeanSquare}(w, t)}$, dividing the gradient by the running RMS magnitude.

nodes.name: Further developments of RMSProp
nodes.statement: Combining RMSProp with standard momentum helps less than usual; combining with Nesterov momentum (Sutskever 2012) works best when the RMS of recent gradients divides the correction rather than the jump; combining with per-connection adaptive learning rates needs more investigation; LeCun's group has a related method (“No more pesky learning rates”).
nodes.origin_citation: Sutskever 2012; LeCun group, “No More Pesky Learning Rates”

nodes.name: Summary of learning methods for neural networks
nodes.statement: For small or non-redundant datasets, prefer full-batch methods (conjugate gradient, LBFGS, adaptive rates, rprop). For big redundant datasets, use mini-batches with momentum, RMSProp (with momentum), or LeCun's recipe; there is no universal recipe because nets and tasks differ widely.
